title: Annapurni Subramaniam Becomes First Indian Woman to Win COSPAR Vikram Sarabhai Medal
excerpt: The astrophysicist and IIA director was honored at the 46th COSPAR Scientific Assembly in Florence for her pioneering contributions to space research and India's AstroSat mission.
body:
• Astrophysicist Annapurni Subramaniam has become the first Indian woman and only the fourth Indian scientist to receive the COSPAR Vikram Sarabhai Medal.
  • The award was presented at the 46th COSPAR Scientific Assembly in Florence, Italy, on August 3, 2026, recognizing her contributions to stellar astronomy and India's AstroSat mission.
  • Subramaniam serves as Director of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru and has published over 175 research papers across a three-decade career.
  • She is also the third woman globally to receive the medal since it was established in 1990.

Annapurni Subramaniam, one of India's leading astrophysicists, has been awarded the COSPAR Vikram Sarabhai Medal for 2026 — becoming the first Indian woman scientist and the fourth Indian overall to receive the prestigious international honor.

The medal was presented at the 46th COSPAR Scientific Assembly in Florence, Italy, on August 3, according to multiple Indian science publications. Subramaniam is also only the third woman globally to earn the distinction since the award was instituted in 1990.

A Career Built Around Stars

Born in Palakkad, Kerala, Subramaniam developed an early fascination with the night sky. She completed her schooling at Victoria College in Palakkad before earning her PhD from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) in 1996, with a thesis on star clusters and stellar evolution.

Over a career spanning more than three decades, she has published over 175 scientific papers on stellar populations, star clusters, blue straggler stars, and the Magellanic Clouds. She has supervised 15 doctoral scholars and mentored numerous young researchers.

Subramaniam currently serves as Director of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru, a position she has held since 2019 — making her the first woman to lead the institution. She also holds additional charge as Director of the Centre for Nano and Soft Matter Sciences (CeNS).

"I am extremely happy to receive this award. This is in recognition of my contribution to research in astrophysics, Indian space mission AstroSat, next-generation astronomy facilities and sustainable development."

— Annapurni Subramaniam

Key Role in AstroSat and Beyond

One of Subramaniam's most notable contributions was serving as the calibration scientist for the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) aboard AstroSat, India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, launched by ISRO in 2015. She carried out the in-orbit performance verification phase, ensuring the telescope operated with precision.

Beyond AstroSat, she has contributed to the international Thirty Metre Telescope (TMT) project, in which India is a participating partner, and leads the proposed next-generation UV-Optical space telescope project called INSIST. She has also supported the development of the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve in Ladakh, one of India's most important sites for astronomical observation.

A Medal With Deep Indian Roots

The COSPAR Vikram Sarabhai Medal is jointly awarded by the Committee on Space Research (COSPAR) and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). It was established in 1990 in honor of Vikram Sarabhai, widely regarded as the father of India's space program.

The medal recognizes scientists from developing countries for outstanding contributions to space research. Previous Indian recipients include U.R. Rao (1996), Gurbax Singh Lakhina (2014), and Anil Bhardwaj (2024).

Recognition and Legacy

Subramaniam's accolades extend beyond this medal. In 2024, she received the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar — Vigyan Shri in the Space Science and Technology category, one of India's highest scientific honors. She is a Fellow of the Indian Academy of Sciences and an active member of the International Astronomical Union.

For the Indian diaspora, Subramaniam's achievement carries particular resonance. Indian-origin scientists and engineers play significant roles in global space agencies, from NASA to ESA, and her recognition at the highest levels of international space research underscores the depth of talent emerging from Indian scientific institutions.

The award citation acknowledged her outstanding contributions to space research in developing countries, highlighting work that spans stellar evolution, ultraviolet astronomy, and the design of future telescope missions.
